maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a
question of privilege. The matter has reference to an editorial which appears in the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, February 16, 1927, entitled: The Byng-King Correspondence; Some Secret History. I would have referred to this matter yesterday, when it first came to my attention, had it not been that my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), was -about to deliver the budget address, and I thought the House would not wish to be detained at that time. I may say that were it not that the article is being copied in other papers throughout this country, -and has also been telegraphed abroad, I would be prepared to treat it with the silent contempt which I accord most of the editorials which appear in the Ottawa Journal in reference to myself. However, -as the article, apart from constituting a reflection on the personal honour of the farmer Governor General of this country, is in the nature of things and as a matter of fact, a fabrication from beginning to end, I feel that as it relates to an important constitutional question, I must make a very clear and emphatic statement concerning it.
I say in the first place that the article in the nature of things is a fabrication, because it implies that the former Governor General was prepared to accord to the Journal the

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
right of listening in on conversations which took place between the Governor General of Canada and the Prime Minister of this country, conversations which in the nature of things were in the strictest confidence. In the second place, it implies that the Governor General was prepared to make to the Journal, or to other persons, statements which he was not prepared to make a matter of official record, and in fact did not make a matter of record in correspondence which admittedly was designed for purposes of official record and to which alone this parliament and the people of this country at the present or at any subsequent time can appeal as the authoritative record. As a matter of fact the article is untrue, as I am in a position authoritatively to state. I shall not read the entire article, but I will refer to one or two pertinent paragraphs. Near the close of the first paragraph the article has the following:
Publication of the letters, however,-
Referring to the correspondence which was laid on the table of the Housemakes it possible, and indeed desirable, to reveal what the letters do not disclose, but what was the very heart and centre of the whole difficulty. The Journal, therefore, herewith presents the exact circumstances which led up to and which justified-the action of Lord Byng.
The action referred to being the refusal of dissolution to myself as Prime Minister last year. I may just note in passing that the use of the words "and which justified" would seem to indicate that even in the mind of the editor of this paper, so far as the official record is concerned, the Governor General's action on constitutional grounds was not justified.
The paragraph that I wish particularly to bring to the attention of the House and to refer to is the following:
To understand and appreciate the position taken by Lord Byng, in refusing Mr. King dissolution, it is necessary to go back to October, 1925. Following the election of that time, which saw Mr. King return to parliament with 16 fewer supporters than Mr. Meighen, Mr. King went down to Rideau Hall and intimated to Lord Byng that he intended to resign. Three or four days later, however, (after he had consulted with his ministers, who told him that he must not resign), Mr. King visited Lord Byng again and told him that he had changed his mind, that he thought it was his duty to meet parliament and to take a chance of surviving a non-confidence motion. Lord Byng, naturally surprised, in view of what Mr. King had said to him at their previous meeting, told Mr. King that he would agree to having him meet parliament, but he added that he thought it should be understood-[DOT]

And then the following appears in italics- *-that in the event of his (Mr. King's) government being defeated, either upon the meeting of parliament, or upon a later date in the session, or in the event of Mr. King finding himself unable to govern, he (Lord Byng) would consider it his duty to call upon Mr. Meighen to find out whether or not he could form a ministry.
The italics end there and the article goes on:
Mr. King said that was perfectly satisfactory.
__ Lord Byng thereupon suggested that Mr. King make this understanding known to his cabinet, and Mr. King said that he would do so. The matter rested there until toward the end of June, 1926.
Following adverse votes against his government in the House of Commons toward the end of June, Mr. King went to Lord Byng-and said that in the circumstances, he would have to advise him to dissolve parliament, Lord Byng at once reminded him of their understanding ...
Fortunately as respects adverse votes against the government, there are the journals of this parliament to appeal to and I repeat what has been repeated time and again, that there was no adverse vote against the government of which I was Prime Minister in the last parliament nor is there record of any to be found in the journals of the House.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext: The records of this House speak for themselves on this point.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext:
The next point to which I wish to refer is the repeated reference in the editorial to an alleged understanding between Lord Byng and myself arrived at after the election of 1925. I wish to say emphatically, on my responsibility as Prime Minister of this country, that there was no understanding between Lord Byng and myself other than what appeared in the public prints of this country in a statement which I issued to the public, after having submitted it to Lord Byng in the first instance for his approval. There was no understanding of any kind, and I cannot make that statement too emphatic nor too clear. The only advice which I tendered to Lord Byng was to let parliament decide with respect to the situation that arose after the election of 1925. That advice was accepted by Lord Byng, and parliament met and did decide the question as to who was to be the leader in this House in the last parliament.
I hold in my hand a statement which I gave to the press on the night of November 4th. This particular statement-

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext: What year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING CORRESPONDENCE WITH LORD BYNG
speechtext:
Nineteen
twenty-five. The election took place on October 29. This statement was handed to the press on the night of November 4, and will be found, I think, in the press of the day following. Before giving this statement to the press I took it personally to government house and presented it to the then Governor General who approved it in its entirety. It was then given to the press; it appeared in the press of our country, and from that moment to this, no exception whatever from any source has been taken to it. The statement is as follows:
The latest official returns having made it apparent that as a result of the general election held on October 29, no one of the participating political parties would of itself have a clear majority in the House when parliament assembles, it became my duty as Prime Minister to acquaint His Excellency the Governor General with the situation and to advise His Excellency as to the course which should be pursued. After several interviews with His Excellency at which the position brought about by the recent general election was fully discussed and all alternatives presented. I have taken the responsibility of advising His Excellency to summon parliament for the earliest practicable date in order to ascertain the attitude of the parliamentary representatives towards the very important question raised by the numerical position of the respective political parties. His Excellency has been pleased to accept this advice.
After careful consideration of the constitutional precedents and their bearing upon the situation which has arisen as a result of the general election, the cabinet decided unanimously this afternoon that it was their constitutional duty to meet parliament at the earliest possible moment, regard being had for the legal requirements with respect to the time necessary for the return of the writs and the official gazetting of the members who have been elected.
In the interval, until parliament assembles it is the intention of the government to refrain from making appointments beyond such as are essential for the proper carrying on of the public business.
In the present situation there are three possible courses of procedure, each of which has been carefully considered by the cabinet:
1.	That His Excellency be asked to grant an immediate dissolution of parliament.
2.	That His Excellency be asked to call upon the leader of the largest political group to form a government.
3.	That His Excellency be asked to summon parliament at the earliest practicable date for the purpose aforementioned.
With respect to an immedate dissolution it was felt that it was not in the interests of the country to occasion the turmoil and expense of another general election until at least parliament had been summoned, and the people's representatives in parliament had been afforded an opportunity of giving expression to their views.
With respect to the leader of the political party having the largest definite following in
the House of Commons being called upon to form an administration, the cabinet holds the view that responsible self-government in Canada rests upon the principle that the majority are entitled to govern, the majority so understood meaning not the political party or group having the largest number of members, but the majority as determined by the duly elected representatives of the people in parliament. Far from indicating that Mr. Meighen is in a position to command a majority in the newly elected House of Commons, the results of the election appear clearly to indicate that he is not in such a position. I am not aware of any precedent in Great Britain or in Canada for recommending, before parliament meets, that the leader of a party not commanding a clear majority in the House of Commons should be called upon to form a government.
To summon parliament and to allow the House of Commons to disclose its attitude upon division, is the procedure warranted by constitutional precedent and by the present circumstances. To take any other course would be to fail to recognize the supreme right of the people to govern themselves in the manner *which the constitution has provided, namely by expressing their will through their duly elected representatives in parliament and in accordance with recognized parliamentary practice.
I wish to repeat that before that statement was given to the press, the very sheets from which I have read the statement and which I now hold in my 'hand and to which I have attached a memorandum of identification, were read by His Excellency the then Governor General, and His Excellency approved the statement exactly in the form in which I have now read it. May I say that the implication of the article in question is that there was some sort of a bargain between the Governor General of this country and myself as Prime Minister whereby I was to hold or be permitted to hold office. Any implication of that kind is a reflection upon the Governor General as the representative of His Majesty the King and a reflection upon myself as Prime Minister. Moreover, it entirely ignores, what at least anyone sitting on this side of the House would maintain as the only constitutional position, and indeed the position which I have stated over and over again to be the constitutional position, namely, that the power to govern in this country comes not from the Governor General but from the people of the country through their representatives in this parliament. That was the one and only position which I as Prime Minister took in conversations with Lord Byng as the Governor General, and it was the basis of the advice which I then gave His Excellency regarding the summoning of parliament and allowing the people's representatives to decide. There was no understanding apart from the advice which I gave in that regard.
May I add that the official record as laid on the table of this House discloses, without the

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
possibility of controversy, that in His Excellency's mind there was no understanding of any kind that could have been directly or indirectly material to, or relevant to, or a salient feature of, the conversations held between us subsequently. If there was any such understanding, it would have been the duty of His Excellency to have made mention of it in correspondence which passed between us and which was for the purpose of having of record exactly what had transpired in conversation. To assume that a Governor General on a great constitutional issue would ignore in an official communication to his Prime Minister the reason which actuated him in taking a particular course is, to imply, to say the least, that the holder of that great office was not competent to fill it. The House I am sure will agree that every pertinent fact with respect to a great constitutional issue, where an official record is being made of the situation, ought to be made a part of the official record.
I wish to read to the House what His Excellency the Governor General wrote me, and I would ask the House to note with care the precise words used in this communication. This letter has already been laid on the table of the House:
Government House, Ottawa,
My dear Mr. King,	June 29, 1926.
I must acknowledge on paper, with many thanks, the receipt of your letter handed to me at our meeting yesterday.
In trying to condense all that has passed between us during the last week, it seems to my mind that there is really only one point at issue.
May I pause to direct the attention of the House to the two phrases used in that sentence:
In trying to condense all that has passed between us.
Note the "all," that is clear and comprehensive. It does not ignore any salient feature, and so as to make it emphatic may I pause to say that Lord Byng, while Governor General, or since has at no time in conversation with me ever alluded to any understanding between himself and myself apart from anything that is of official record here, and this for the good and sufficient reason that there was no understanding apart from what is recorded. Lord Byng continues:
It seems to my mind that there is really only one point at issue.
Only one point, note again the "one." What is the point?
You advise me "that as, in your opinion, Mr. Meighen is unable to govern the country, there should be another election with the present machinery, to enable the people to decide." My contention is-

Not that there was some understanding on which I was holding office, butthat Mr. Meighen has not been given a chance of trying to govern, or saying that he cannot do so, and that all reasonable expedients should be tried before resorting to another election.
Permit me to say once more that, before deciding on my constitutional course on this matter, I gave this subject the most fairminded and painstaking consideration which it was in my power to apply.
I can only add how sincerely I regret the severance of our official companionship and how gratefully I acknowledge the help of your counsel and co-operation.
With warmest wishes,
Yours sincerely,
Byng of Vimy.
To that communication I replied as follows: Ottawa, July 3, 1926. His Excellency, General
The Right Honourable the Lord Byng of Vimy, G.C.B.,	G.C.M.G., etc., Governor
General of the Dominion of Canada, Ottawa.
My dear Lord Byng:
I duly received Your Excellency's letter of June 29th, for which I desire to thank Your Excellency.
Paragraph three of Your Excellency's letter reads as follows:
"You advise me 'that as, in your opinion, Mr. Meighen is unable to govern the country, there should be another election with the present machinery to enable the people to decide'." Also:
"My contention is that Mr. Meighen has not been given a chance of trying to govern, or saying that he cannot do so, and that all reasonable expedients should be tried before resorting to another election."
To the accuracy of the statement of Your Excellency's contention as set forth in this paragraph, I have no exception to take. Inasmuch, however, as what purports to have been my advice to Your Excellency appears in Your Excellency's letter within quotation marks, and might therefore be assumed to be words of mine as expressed in conversation with Your Excellency in tendering advice, may I respectfully say that the words "with the present machinery"-apart from the entire sentence appearing as a quotation,-are quite misleading, as no such words were used or referred to by me in any advice tendered. Fortunately, the text of the quotation clearly indicates that, taken as a whole, the words as quoted could not have been words coming from me.
I advttsed Your Excellency that, in my opinion, the existing situation in the House of Commons demanded a dissolution of parliament, and there should be another election to enable the people to decide upon a new House of Commons.
In reply to Your Excellency's contention that Mr. Meighen had not been given a chance of trying to govern, or saying that he could not do so, I said that I could not advise Your Excellency to send for Mr. Meighen or for any other member of the present House of Commons to form an administration, as I did not

Maritime Claims
believe any other administration could be formed which would command the confidence of the House. As to Mr. Meighen not having been given a chance of trying to govern, I pointed out that at the commencement of the session it had been left to the people's representatives in parliament to decide as to who was to advise Your Excellency, and that Mr. Meighen's chances to obtain the support of the Commons had been quite as good as my own; that the House of Commons having declined to express any confidence in Mr. Meighen throughout the entire session. I could not see wherein there was any probability of the House giving him the support which would enable him to carry on the government, and that therefore I could not assume the responsibility of advising Your Excellency to send for him. As there was still less probability of any other hon. member of the House being able to command its confidence, dissolution, to be followed by a general election, in which the people would be given an opportunity to decide, appeared to me the only course which I could advise, and I advised accordingly.
As no formal record of the conversations between us was kept-
I will ask the House to pay attention to this paragraph, because I was drawing the attention of His Excellency to the advisability of having a record of exactly what was said between us, knowing that this question at some future time would be raised:
As no formal record of the conversations between us was kept, I have felt, in view of the representations of paragraph three of Your Excellency's letter, which will become a matter of official record, I should also record on paper my own statement of the advice tendered Your Excellency both as regards dissolution and Your Excellency's contention in reference thereto.
With respect to the concluding paragraph of Your Excellency's letter, may I say that I am sure that the regret felt by Your Excellency at the severance of our official companionship was not any greater than my own, and that I acknowledge with not less gratitude the help of Your Excellency's counsel and co-operation throughout the period during which I had the privilege of enjoying Your Excellency's confidence.
I am, You Excellency,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Now what was the reply made by His Excellency to that communication, which, as I state, is the official record of wihat took place between us both as regards dissolution and His Excellency's contention in reference thereto. It was as follows:
Government House
Ottawa, July 5th, 1926.
Dear Mr. King,
Many thanks for your letter of July 3rd. The letter in question was written entirely from the wish on my part to express my sincere gratitude. for the help and co-operation you have given me during your tenure of the Premiership. The quotations in it are by no means intended to recall words used at our meetings, and in that connection I would ask you to read the preceding paragraph.
I was stating my impression as to the one point at issue, and endeavouring to put it in a condensed form.
I repeat that statement:
I was stating my impression as to the one point at issue, and endeavouring to put it in a condensed form.
Of course, I readily add your letter to the documentary record of the situation.
Yours sincerely,
Byno of Vimt.
The Rt. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
C.M.G., etc., etc., Ottawa.
There is the official record as given to this parliament of all that actually transpired that was material between Lord Byng and myself, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no public journal in this or any other country has a right to circulate false statements, false representations with respect to communications between the Prime Minister of a country and the representative of His Majesty, and this more especially when it is known that the only source from which the truth can come is either the representative of the crown itself or the Prime Minister of the country with whom the conversations were had.
Again, as Prime Minister of Canada, I wish to repeat that the record as laid on the table of the House here sums up, in its entirety, all of what transpired between Lord Byng and myself in reference to dissolution as respects all salient and essential features.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL

speechtext: The House resumed from February 15th consideration in committee of Bill No. 55, to provide for special control by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs of certain islands in the St. Lawrence river being part of the St. Regis Indian reservation.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: When we discussed this bill, before, I understood that the minister was going to inquire and bring down a memorandum showing the Teasons advanced by the officials of the department why there should be special clauses in this act different from those in the general Indian Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Superintendent General of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
In our discussion of section 2 of the act the other day, the hon. member for Argen-teuil asked why the necessity for its inclusion in this bill, and had we not authority in the Indian Act itself? We have authority in sections 127 and 128 of the Indian Act to prevent the cutting of timber, and penalties are provided for the prosecution of parties who trespass and take off the timber, but the provision in the act applies only to lands occupied by the Indians. That is distinctly stated. I have gone thoroughly into that matter, and that is the reason we are asking for authority here. Where the land is not in occupation by the Indians or owned in common by them we have no authority in the act to prevent the Indians from cutting timber. We want this provision because we are dealing with land which is the common 
property of the band not allocated to any member of the band and not resided on by the Indians. The provision is practically identical with the provision contained in the Indian Act for the' purpose of the prevention of depredations or cutting of timber on land held by allotment.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Since the matter was in
the committee on a previous occasion, my hon. friend from Stormont (Mr. Smith) came to see me and endeavoured to explain what was really behind this special bill. Perhaps if my hon. friend from Cornwall would enlighten the committee it might make the matter clearer, because I think he understands the question better than any other hon. member in the committee.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
These islands
mentioned in Bill No. 55 lie opposite and east of Cornwall. Unfortunately, the other day when the bill was before the committee I was called out of the House. I am very glad it has come up again because it gives me an opportunity to say a few words in regard to it. I have read over the Hansard report covering the questions asked when the bill was before the committee on a previous occasion, and I notice that some hon. member asks if these islands were in any way required for the St. Lawrence development. I may say that all works in connection with the St. Lawrence development are several miles west of these properties. The nearest island is the Easterbrook farm on Cornwall island. That island is occupied by the Indians of the St. Regis reservation, with the exception of one farm, which was leased about 105 or 106 years ago to the Easterbrook family and has been occupied by them ever since. Hamilton's island and Macmaster's island were in the same position, except that they were leased to families of the present tenants and were never occupied by the Indians. Col-quhoun's island which is referred to by another name in the bill is also in the same position. A few years ago the department, feeling that the present tenants were not paying anything like an adequate rental for the property, took action in the Exchequer court to have the leases terminated at the expiration of the first ninety-nine year period. The cases have been in court for some time, and in connection with Maemaster island judgment was given declaring that the leases were not renewable for the next ninety-nine year period. The Colquhoun estate, which held the lease for Colquhoun's island, accepting this as good law, abandoned the island, and threw themselves upon the mercy of the department so far as future leases were concerned. The Easterbrook and Hamil-

St. Regis Indian Reserve
ton island cases are still pending and have not yet been brought to trial, but undoubtedly the same judgment will be given in these cases. Macmaster island was the summer home of the late Sir Donald Macmaster and is not suitable for any other pur-4 p.m. pose. If the Indians were in possession of that island it would be absolutely of no use to them and would not be productive or return any revenue. Hamilton island is a fairly large-sized island. On one end of it there is the Hamilton farm, and on the other end of it there are about thirty-five summer cottages, with some little timber back of the cottages. This island, outside of the one farm on it, would not be suitable to produce any revenue whatever for the Indians, but as a summer resort it is largely used by the people of Cornwall and surrounding districts. Colquhoun's island would not produce anything at all of any value to the Indians of that section, or any other section, but it likewise has some thirty-five to forty' summer cottages. The Easter-brook farm is a farm of about 200 acres on the Cornwall island, and was held by the Easter-brook family and while a good farm is more valuable from a sentimental standpoint. It is not a very convenient location, because they have to cross in small boats to get to market' in Cornwall. The leases were held to be non-renewable. Under the existing regulation the department would have a perfect right to allow the Indians to go on the lands in question but the band would not have a right to lease the property to any particular Indian. The land would be non-productive. These lands would not be of any real value to the Indians, because the Indians, as I know them are anything but thrifty, and the result would 'be that those summer cottages would be destroyed and no rental would be received. The Indians would be content to lead a life of luxury in the cottages so long as they stayed there. The only request I have to make to the department is that if this bill goes through, and if the islands are leased under short term leases, the Indians shall get the benefit of the higher rentals that might be obtained on any renewal of leases. I am content, in order to safeguard the Indians, that a clause should be put in providing that the leases should be for five years, or any short period the department may fix. I heard it mentioned by some hon. member that perhaps there was some motive behind this bill. There has been a rumour that the island is wanted by some American organization for the purpose of constructing an hotel, or something of that description. I would be the first to object to that, because I am very much interested in
the people who have possession of the place now, and who, by the way, are using the place more or less as squatters, and are not paying any rent in the meantime, because the department refuses to accept rent. The department claims that they have no right to be there and they cannot make any lease with them, although there is back rent coming to them since the time the leases were declared to be terminated.
The Indians have been provided with every safeguard in this matter, they have everything to gain by the bill going through and the department obtaining for them a fair rental, and I hope the committee will consent to this measure being passed.

The House resumed, from February 15, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Hon. Mr. Heenan-Mr. Johnston in the chair:

Old Age Pensions
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting old age pensions, and to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may make an agreement with the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province for the payment to such province quarterly of an amount equal to one-half of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions hereinafter specified and regulations made under the proposed legislation.
2.	That every agreement so made shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the Governor General to the Lieutenant-Governor of the province with which the same was made.
3.	That before any agreement so made comes into operation, the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province. and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the Governor in Council.
4.	That all sums payable to any province in pursuance of any such agreement shall be payable from time to time on the certificate of the Minister of Finance out of any moneys belonging to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada not otherwise appropriated.
5.	That provision shall be made for the payment of a pension to every person who, at the date of the proposed commencement of the pension:-
(a)	is a British subject, or, being a widow, was such before her marriage;
(b)	has attained the age of seventy years;
(e) has resided in Canada for the twenty
years immediately preceding the date aforesaid ;
(d)	has resided in the province in which the application for pension is made for the five years immediately preceding the said date;
(e)	is not an Indian as defined by the Indian Act;
(f)	has not made any voluntary assignment or transfer of property for the purpose of qualifying for a pension.
_ 6. That the receipt of a pension shall not by itself constitute a disqualification from voting at any provincial or municipal election.
7.	That the maximum pension payable shall be two hundred and forty dollars yearly, which shall be subject to reduction by the amount of the income of the pensioner in excess of one hundred and twenty-five dollars a year.
8.	That provisions be made as to the credit to the pension authority of the annual value of a pensioner's residence, and the recovery of pension payments out of deceased pensioner's estate, and for the distribution of pension burden among provinces by proportionate reimbursement or proportionate reduction where the pensioner resided in more than one province or transfers his permanent residence to another province, and for ceasing of payments where he transfers his residence to some place out of Canada, and the revival of his rights upon again becoming a resident of Canada.
9.	That no pension shall be subject to alienation or transfer by the pensioner, or to seizure in satisfaction of any claim against him.
10.	That on or before the thirtieth day of April in each year, the Minister of Finance shall make a full report to parliament of the operation of the agreements made pursuant to the proposed act, and of the moneys of Canada paid to the provinces under each of the several agreements entered into pursuant thereto.
11.	That the Governor in Council shall have power from time to time, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, and with the approval of the Treasury board, to make regulations, not inconsistent with the provisions of the proposed act, with regard to the pensions herein provided for, and such regulations shall be published in the Canada Gazette, and be laid before parliament.

This is the proper time to offer criticisms or suggestions in regard to the subject of old age pensions. We should be in a better position to discuss this matter this year, because in the meantime we have passed through a general election in which this question was considered by hon. gentlemen opposite to be one of the main issues. We on this side of the House were charged with opposing the principle of old age pensions and with actually killing the bill. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who were here last year will agree that these charges are not well founded. We offered criticism, as we have a perfect right to do, but the bill passed' the House without a division. In my own campaign I was very unfairly charged with opposing this principle, and in that connection I wish to refer to two general statements which I made when the matter was being considered last year. At page 2537 of Hansard I said:
There is probably one point on which we all agree, and that is that something is necessary in the way of old age pension legislation.
Then further on, at page 2538, I made another general statement:
Now, at the present time we know that from all over the Dominion there is a call from many aged people for immediate relief, and I am of opinion that the source of that relief should be the federal government...
Throughout the campaign I adopted the same position which I am adopting to-day and which I took last year.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) on his appointment to the important post of Minister of Labour, but considering his long experience with social legislation I am somewhat surprised that he did not bring down a bill a little more acceptable to the country; I had hoped that he would have fathered a federal scheme. In fairness to all parts of Canada I am convinced that old age pensions should be administered by the federal government, but the minister has decided otherwise, and according to the resolution before the House
Old Age Pensions

the bill will be the same as that passed last year, in spite of the announced opposition of a majority of the provinces. I think I am safe in saying that, from the replies read the other day by the minister. He followed the reading of those letters by a statement, which I did not quite understand; he said:
If in view of these replies, we now introduce a bill that removes the obstacles mentioned, would you not consider that the provinces are in favour of an old age pension scheme?
Further on he said:
As an example, the province of British Columbia was opposed to this scheme because the obstacles in the way were insurmountable, but to-day we have the spectacle of a bill introduced in the legislature providing for this on a co-operative plan.
The minister said British Columbia was opposed to this bill because there were insurmountable obstacles in its path, but I think hon. gentlemen will agree that these obstacles could not have been removed by the legislation, because he tells us that the bill is similar to that passed last year. Then why did the Premier of British Columbia adopt the scheme? He did so simply because he considered it a good weapon to use in the interests of the Liberal party in the last election. He toured the province during that campaign in the interests of the Liberal candidates, and promised the electors that he would bring down legislation accepting a federal scheme; he also advised them that it was in their interests to send to Ottawa Liberal members. Mr. Oliver kept his word so far as the bill was concerned, but apparently the electors did not accept his advice. The Minister of Labour, in referring to the fact that this was one of the main issues of the campaiign said:
If we are to interpret the will of the electorate on that question in the way we usually interpret electoral decisions, there can be no question that the principle adopted in this Bill was endorsed by the people of Canada.
I wonder how he interprets the results in British Columbia? I will undertake to do that for him, in a very few words. I passed through that campaign, and I am convinced that the people of that province are favourable to old age pensions, but they are not favourable to the bill introduced last session.
In view of the fact that we cannot have a federal measure, and since British Columbia is willing to accept something in the way of a co-operative scheme, as one of the representatives of that province I am prepared to accept such legislation if it is made fair and reasonable, but I am going to offer a few suggestions which I think would make the proposed bill a little more acceptable.

Dealing first with clause 5 of the resolution, it is proposed to set the age limit at 70 years. If this age limit were in force in Australia, where the limit is now 65, we are informed that 90 per cent of those now in receipt of an old age pension would not receive anything. In New Zealand the disparity is even greater. There the limit is 65 for males and 60 for females, which limit may be reduced to 60 and 55 respectively where two or more children under fourteen are dependent on the recipient of the pension. Just in connection with this point I would like to quote an extract from a letter appearing in a Vancouver paper which reached me to-day. The letter deals with this matter and is signed by an ex-soldier:
In regard to the proposed pension bill now being advocated, surely some clause should be inserted or brought up giving special privileges to the returned soldier who has prematurely aged through war service. The present act stipulates at the age of 70, but I would venture to say that many of us, especially those like myself who perhaps were not wounded but suffered from camp life and exposure, will not last out to this age and, moreover, if living to the age of 00, will be unable to carry on work in civil life. These are the ones who surely deserve special consideration in a scheme of old age pensions.
I would suggest to the minister that he consider the scheme adopted in New Zealand whereby the age limit may be reached in certain cases.
Clause 7 of the resolution provides for a maximum pension of $20 per month, as compared with $26.50 in Australia. In this connection I would like to draw attention to .another letter appearing recently in the Vancouver press:
...you credit Premier Oliver with being a generous man. Is the following a sample of his generosity? He was reported as saying he is in favour of the old age pension bill of $20 per month for men of 70 years, as passed by members of the Commons and, moreover, was cited as saying "Half a loaf is better than none." And that in face of the fact that prisoners in British Columbia jails are allowed $1 per day for their upkeep by the British Columbia government and no room rent to pay.
What on earth could our poor old indigent men do with $20 per month? The lowest price for a small, clean bedroom in Vancouver is $2.50 per week. That figures out at $11.17 per month and would leave them $8.83 to buy food for thirty-one days, and would mean slow starvation. Why such discrimination against our aged poor? The eligible age should be 65, the same as in England, Australia and other countries, and the pension not less than criminals in British Columbia jails are receiving for their upkeep, $1 per day.
I would urge that the minister give a little consideration to the advisability of increasing

Old Age Pensions
this pension. I also point out that the resolution only permits a pensioner to have an income of $125 per annum. Now New Zealand is much more generous in the matter of private income. It permits the pensioner to have an income up to $390 per annum or $650 if the recipient is married, and the net value of accumulated property may be as high as $2,000.
But the clause to which I take the greatest exception is the one which provides that on the death of the pensioner his home or his estate shall be sold, and the total amount of the pension plus five per cent compounded annually, shall be taken out and placed to the credit of the pension authority, in this case the government. Five per cent compounded annually! The minister will find that is a greater rate than many of the loan companies charge.
In the proposed legislation we are asked to set aside certain sums to be paid out of this pension to a certain class of people. Before the session closes we shall be called upon to vote from the revenue of this country over $38,000,000 under the heading of pensions. It is true that of this amount something over $37,000,000 may be termed war pensions, and that over $1,000,000 is to provide pensions to other classes authorized by statute. I take no exception to the granting of these pensions. No doubt they are given in recognition of service rendered or of sacrifices made. But the same claim holds good in the case of the very class that we are concerned with to-day -the old people of our land who suffered hardships and made many sacrifices in carrying on the pioneer work of this country. They have passed through the earning period of their lives, and through misfortune are in need of assistance. That assistance should come from the state, and I believe the pension is the proper form it should take. But does the Minister of Labour think that this paltry $20 a month would take care of an aged person who is without a home, who has no income, who is in fact destitute? Is this pension intended to supply all the necessaries of life, such as rent, fuel, food and a few comforts? I think not. The provinces will be called upon to look after the majority of these cases in their institutions as they have in the past. I do agree however that this small amount will greatly assist, particularly in cases where the recipient has a home and a small income.
Now I come back to paragraph 8 of the resolution dealing with the recovery of pension payments out of a deceased pensioner's estate. Is there such a condition enforced in the case of the pensioner who will benefit from the
vote of $38,000,000 to which I have already referred, which will stand as a charge against the estates of these pensioners? No, there is not, I do not think anyone would wish that there should be such a provision, although no doubt in a large number of oases the recipients have comfortable homes and in many cases fairly large incomes. Why then should the pension in this case stand as a first mortgage against the class that we are considering to-day? This clause really changes the pension into a loan, and I would strongly urge the minister to consider cutting the paragraph out. Or if he insists on leaving it in, let him apply the words which he himself used the other day and change the title of this bill to "Old Age Loan Bill". Because the clause in question makes the pension a loan secured by a first mortgage bearing a rate of five per cent compounded annually.

Supposing the aged father or mother should have a son who is fairly well off but refuses to take care of the parent, and the pension authority was called upon to award a pension of $240. If the aged people had their own home the pension authority would never ask them to leave their home, but when they died does my hon. friend think that their property or estate should go to that son?
No.
The clause is intended to meet a case of that character.
I understand that in this province, as well as in the province of Nova Scotia, the provincial statutes make the sons or daughters responsible for the care of the aged parents.
In British Columbia also.

I should like to answer that question in this way: Suppose that an old man, one of our early pioneers, who is past the earning period of his life has been able to save sufficient to secure a little home and garden for himself, but feels that he should have some assistance, and in fact is in need of it. Under this legislation you say to that man, "We will give you a pension but it will be only in the form of a mortgage on your home". That old man would consider such a restriction very unfair. As a citizen he should have the privilege of doing what he likes with his home; it is not likely that he would leave it to the son who has refused to come to his assistance although he might bequeath it to an institution or to some per-
Old Age Pensions

son who was in need. Such a provision is very inadvisable. As I said before it changes this measure from a pension bill to a loan bill.

I point out to my hon. friend that subsection 3 of section 9 will meet such a case as he has described.
, Mr. BARBER: I do not think it covers it exactly.
It is intended to cover it.
I think the minister will find that it does not meet such a case. I assure my hon. friend that I am offering these remarks in a kindly spirit.
I am sure of that.

I am prepared to give the minister all the support possible, but I hope he will consider the suggestions I have made so that when we are considering the bill in committee of the whole he will be prepared to make amendments in the direction indicated.
Mr. W OOD6WORTH:	We labour representatives have all along been in favour of a federal measure. That was shown very clearly two yearn ago when my colleague Mr. Irvine, proposed an amendment to that effect. However, as the government undertook last year to introduce a measure along the lines recommended by the parliamentary committee of three years ago, we felt that the best thing we could do was to support the measure then introduced and endeavour to make as great a success of it -as possible. At that time it was not apparent that any of the provinces were in favour of this or any other old age pension scheme. It was not clear that the members of the House were in favour of any old age pension scheme. In the vote to which I referred just now the older parties had united in opposing a federal scheme. Therefore we felt that the only thing ito do was to take a half loaf, and we hoped that this scheme would produce at least some good and that, once it was placed on the statute books, it might ultimately be amended so as to bring it more in harmony with our ideals.
I can see some advantages in having the provinces administer the act. In that way there will be in the administration a certain check which might not be present if the machinery were handled directly from Ottawa. Nearly all the provinces have already administrative machinery which might be utilized for this purpose, and therefore it would not be necessary to set up duplicate machinery. On the other hand, I think that in principle men or women ought to be

eligible for this pension, not merely because they happen to be living in a particular province which has adopted the scheme, but because they are citizens of Canada.
I would, however, suggest that if the federal government has finally decided upon a cooperative scheme, it should be willing to grant say 75 'per cent of the amount. That is frankly a compromise, but it is a compromise that would add greatly to the efficacy of the bill. I am afraid that if the bill is put through in this form, it may not be operative in all the provinces. Since we had the discussion in this House last year, I had an opportunity of meeting citizens of nearly all the provinces from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I found that in the east, especially down in the maritime provinces, it was very doubtful if the provinces would adopt the scheme if it were put on a fifty-fifty basis. We are anxious to have a scheme that will be operative, that will be effective, and I would suggest that we -would ensure that much more effectively if the Dominion government could see its way to give 75 per cent of the amount As the House knows, we private members are precluded from bringing in an amendment along that line, but we would earnestly press this action upon the government. The government is quite safe. The official opposition has already expressed itself as favourable to a federal scheme, but as prepared to - support some such scheme as this if it is impossible to put through a federal scheme.
There is no measure which has received such popular support across the country as has the old age pension scheme. In almost every province it was one of the foremost subjects for discussion in the recent election. Even away down in the east, in Nova Scotia, where I say that it may be difficult to put the scheme into operation, I was told by the editor of one of the leading Conservative newspapers that undoubtedly this was the most important election issue in that province. Under these circumstances the government ought to feel justified in going a great deal further than it did a year ago.
The "situation has altogether changed within the past year. Sometimes if we re-introduce the old measure, we are going as far as we did last year. Sometimes when the situation is altogether changed, a re-introduction of the identical measure is by no means as venturesome a proposal as was that of a year ago. Hon. members will remember that in Through a Looking Glass the queen is made to say to Alice: "Now, here, you see, it takes all the running you can do to keep in the same place." I am suggesting that if the government wants to maintain the same

Royal Assent
place before the public that it occupied when it introduced this measure a year ago, it ought very distinctly to improve the measure.
I should like to endorse a great deal that has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Barber) with regard to the various particulars in the bill. I believe the age ought to be lowered. Especially in industry among the people who will most need these pensions, a man is not worth very much by the time he passes the age of forty or forty-five. That is a most lamentable state of affairs, but none the less it is true that in a large number of industries when a man gets beyond the age of forty or forty-five, younger men are preferred and he often finds it difficult to hold his accustomed job. Long before he reaches the age of seventy he is a burden upon himself or upon the community. As we know, under modem conditions when men shift about necessarily from job to job there is no sense of responsibility on the part of the individual employer. There perhaps have been a dozen or twenty or fifty employers in the course of a man's life, so that no one employer feels really responsible when the man reaches the age of seventy years. Under those conditions of modern industry it seems only right that the state should assume its share of responsibility.
Again I would suggest that a larger amount should be granted, but more particularly a larger sum should be permitted as outside income which a man may receive without his being disqualified to receive a pension. If a man is capable of doing a little work on the side, he ought to be able to do work to the extent of more than $125 a year or to have property that would bring him in an income of more than $125 a year without being disqualified from receiving a pension of this character. I compare the treatment that we are meting out to these pensioners with that which we mete out to our higher public officials. I think of those to whom the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) referred a year ago, namely our judges and many of that type who are receiving large incomes from private sources and who yet are not debarred from receiving large pensions from the public treasury. There ought to be something like equality in dealing with matters of this kind.
Farther, h, ptrrticu'lar modification which might readily be made by the Minister of Labour is that if a man has been living in his younger days in a province in which the pension is operative and has moved to a province in which it is not operative, he ought to be able to draw at least the government portion for the whole of his time. I do not see why if he
moves from one province! to another the entire 50 per cent that should be paid by the government should be cut off, but wherever he is living, whether or not the province has been donating to this fund, he should not receive the entire federal contribution. I think that is an eminently fair amendment which could very readily be made, and will be quite in keeping with the whole tenor of the bill.
There is another matter upon which I should very much like to have an expression from the minister, and that is with regard to the possible revision of this bill. We have been told that once we get it on the statute books, it will be quite possible to make revisions later, possibly in the way of granting a larger amount or some amendment of that sort. It does seem to me however that this bill is something in the nature of a contract between the Dominion government and the provinces, and I would like to be sure-I hope the minister will make this very clear-that the bill can be readily modified even if all the provinces are not in favour of such a modification. We ought not to enter into any permanent arrangements in a matter of this kind, but rather leave the way open so that without any great amount of red tape we might bring in such modifications as time shows to be desirable.
In conclusion, I would repeat that it seems to me that if the government is sincere in hoping for the success of this bill, and I have no reason whatever to believe they are not, they would seriously consider the giving of a much larger proportion by the federal treasury than is now provided for.

The House resumed in committee consideration of the resolution respecting old age pensions, Mr. Johnston iin the chair.

I rise to make some
(Observations on the provisions of this bill, in the spirit of constructive suggestion, which have come to me as a result of the last general election. It is well known that the old age pension bill was an important concern, if not the chief concern, of the masses of the people during the recent general election. All kinds of arguments and suggestions were presented; sometimes not very fair criticisms were made by each side one against the other, and in some constituencies some of >the most worthy and excellent membei-s of the government were veTy nearly defeated on account of the provisions of the old age pension bill, and it is those provisions which I now seek to correct if the minister will listen to suggestions. Section 2 of the resolution deals with the question of the agreement in force between the federal and provincial governments, and states that the agreement shall remain in force so long as the provincial

statute remains in operation, or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the Governor General to the Lieutenant-Governor of the province with which the same was made. I make the suggestion that there is an uncertainty in that provision which is not necessary. It means that, through political conditions or political manoeuvres, it is possible that some province may undertake to enter into an agreement on which the people entitled to receive old age pensions will depend, and they may depend that it will remain in force for a number of years, and yet that province, perhaps after some election, can terminate that measure immediately without notice. It would be just as easy for the minister or the government to provide in this measure for notice on the part of the province as they have provided for notice on the part of the federal government. The federal government are required to give ten years' notice from which date a notice to terminate the agreement is made. My suggestion is that there should be twenty years' notice provided for on the part of both the provincial and the federal government. The reason why I make this suggestion is this. A man of seventy who has been receiving his pension has after ten yeans come to rely upon that pension, and at the age of eighty having made no other provision, the ordinary charitable or benevolent institutions having become less or gone out of existence, through the political manoeuvres or machinations of some government that man may find himself without a pension. I think if the principle of old age pension is to be adopted in Canada it should be made certain and definite, not only so far as governments are concerned, but so far as beneficiaries are concerned.
My first point is that if definite notice of a term of years on the part of the Dominion government be necessary, it should also be necessary so far as the province is concerned, and I make the suggestion that twenty years' notice should be required under the terms of the agreement entered into between the province and the Dominion. I have before me the bill which has been recently presented to the legislature of British Columbia, Bill No. 12, an act to provide for old age pensions. Clause 2 deals with the question of the agreement with the Dominion and I ask the minister to note it, because it affects the other provinces, British Columbia being the first province to enter into this arrangement. That clause reads:
The Lieutenant Governor in Council may enter into an agreement with the Governor Gen-

Old Age Pensions
eral in Council as to a general scheme of old age pensions in the province pursuant to the provisions of any act of the Dominion heretofore or hereafter passed relating to old age pensions

What is the hon. member
reading from?

From the bill recently
presented to, and I presume now before, the legislature of British Columbia, and the point is that the essential feature of the bill is the authority of the Lieutenant Governor in Council to enter into agreement with the Governor General in Council under the terms provided by the legislation. Let the federal parliament take advantage of this recommendation and make their terms. Let them stipulate for ten years' notice and make it a part of the agreement. It will necessarily be a part of the piovincial statute. The next point I make is with reference to clause 5 of the resolution, and I direct the ministers attention to the absence of the subsection between (e) and (f) which formerly existed in the bill. I refer to Bill No. 21 which passed the House of Commons 28th May, 1926. That bill, clause 8, subsection 1 (f), provided that a person would be entitled to a pension if he were not in receipt of an income of as much as 8365 a year. In the resolution before the House that clause is omitted, and I would ask the minister if I may, at this stage, the reason why that clause is left out, because without that clause a person with an income of $25,000 a year may ask for old age pension.

The resolution does not
contain all the provisions of the bill. There are, I think, about eleven clauses in the resolution whereas there are about twenty clauses in the bill.

As regards that item the
resolution is specific; there are the subsections from (a) to (f) which are precisely in the words of the previous bill. This is something that will form an important feature of the bill.
It is contained in the bill.

That is all right, then.
Subsection (a) of section 5 provides for the payment of a pension to any person who is a British subject or, being a widow, was such before her marriage. The Minister of Health (Mr. King, Kootenay) and I had a considerable discussion on that point. He charged me in the province of British Columbia with not having frankly stated the matter to the people. In the case of a woman married to an alien who has become naturalized, I suggest that if the alien is from a country where there is dual nationality-that is to say, where a person retains the citizenship of his country of origin even though he may have become naturalized in Canada, for example -it is possible that such a woman if she became a widow might not be entitled to any pension, notwithstanding that the act might intend her to have one. The minister should consult the Department of Justice on that question with respect to people from countries with dual nationality. Under international law a serious point might arise in that connection. I have not gone deeply into that particular phase of the matter, but I believe that there is some danger in that direction.
Another important feature of the bill has reference to the age at which people are to become entitled to pensions. The bill categorically fixes the age at seventy. I strongly impress upon the minister the fact that if the spirit of the legislation is observed it will not be possible to determine eligibility for pension merely by a consideration of the number of years a person has lived, for many people are old at sixty-much older than others who have actually lived seventy years. The proposed method of determining when the pension should be payable is not a sound one. I suggest that it might be advisable to fix an arbitrary age at seventy and allow the pension authorities some discretion to determine whether in particular cases people at the age of sixty or sixty-five, by reason of physical infirmities or because of other conditions that justify it, should be entitled to consideration. I do not know any other practical method of meeting this difficulty. If you fix upon the age of seventy arbitrarily, you rule out many thousands of aged and worthy people who ought to receive pensions because of ill health after a long life of hard work. In Australia where the age limit is sixty-five-I ask the minister to note this particularly-ninety per cent of those in receipt of pensions would get nothing if the limit were fixed at seventy. This shows the far-reaching effect of the principle I am pointing out. To fix an arbitrary limit of seventy virtually rules out ninety per cent of the people who, in my opinion, should be given pensions. In Australia, it is said, of 105,000 persons receiving pensions a little over ninety per cent are under seventy; and in New Zealand the limit is fixed much lower. Australia has a smaller population than ours.
My hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth) has discussed the question of removal from one province to another. The legislation as
Old Age Pensions

it stands does present a handicap to any pensioner -moving from one locality to another in the Dominion. Suppose the pensioner lives in Saskatchewan, a healthy place to live in. For good reasons the doctor may order him to go to a milder province like British Columbia. And because of that removal the pensioner's allowance is cut down. This is wrong in principle, and this very fact constitutes an argument in favour of a federal scheme. In my opinion, to have a really workable pension system in Canadr it must be federal in its scope, because many of the provinces will never come in, and those that do will be faced with such restrictions as will make it difficult for pensioners to get the benefit of the legislation. I have already spoken with regard to the question of income.

The hon. member misinterprets the provision. Section 4 provides that any pensioner removing to another province with which no agreement under the act is in force shall continue to be paid the pension by the province in which it was granted.
I refer to the section relative to a transfer of residence as between two provinces both of which are in the scheme.

If a person at the age of
sixty-five moves from Saskatchewan to British Columbia, say, having no claim in British Columbia but one in Saskatchewan, that person loses a part of his pension, as I understand the bill.
Yes.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to what I consider a fatal defect in the proposed legislation, and that is the virtual confiscation of property belonging to the aged. A discussion took place a short time ago between my hon. friend (Mr. Barber) and the minister on that point, and although the minister may not officially admit it I am sure he knows from his contact with people that if there is one objectionable feature to the old age pensions bill which strikes the average pertson with a sense of revulsion it is the provision that thrifty people who have worked hard during their lives and put by a little money in order to buy a home, may be faced with the prospect that after their death some dependent, for whom they have provided what little they can, will be deprived of the benefit of their economy. They may have saved up money to provide the means of education and under this legislation the pension authorities can levy out of the property the amount of the pension paid, plus five per cent interest per annum, compounded. I

heard the minister's suggestion of the wealthy son or daughter who was unwilling to assist the old folks, and who finally inherited property from the deceased pensioner. It is conceivable that such cases may arise, but the other class of cases will also occur. You may have an aged lady looking after a granddaughter whose future education she may have in view; she may be anxious to send that girl to high school or to normal school or to have her educated in some other way. The old lady dies and the government steps in and says. "We will take the property and the child can go to the orphans' home." Surely it is within the resources of the minister to find something more just under the circumstances. In Australia they allow a maximum amount of property of $2,000. That is one method of getting over it. It could be suggested that if the property is going to people in affluent circumstances who, having a duty to look after their parents have failed to do so, the State would then have priority, but to pass a clause of this kind which confiscates the property under all circumstances, or practically all circumstances, is unjust, inequitable and unnecessary.

I assume the hon. member to be familiar with the bill we had last year, which says:
[DOT] [DOT] .no claim shall be made by a pension authority for the recovery of such debt directly or indirectly out of any part of the pensioner's estate which passes by will or on an intestacy to any other pensioner or to any person who has, since the grant of such pension or for the last three years during which such pension has continued to be paid, regularly contributed to the support of the pensioner by the payment of money or otherwise to an extent which, having regard to the means of the person so having contributed, is considered by the pension authority to be reasonable.
In. other words, if someone has contributed to the upkeep of this pensioner, the government has no claim whatever.
But that does not cover the point I am making. That section only says that a person who has assumed the duty of the state-
No.

That is what it means, a person who has assisted the old people; to such ia person the state says "We will not come in and take the money; we will let you get your money back first and then we will take ours." That is not the point I am making. No government would suggest that if the old people wanted to pay back a son or daughter who had given money in place of the pension, the government should have

Old Age Pensions
any priority. I am dealing with the case where an old couple or an old person may have a home worth $2,000', which they desire to leave to some grandchild who may be an infant. Under this provision the pension authorities would step in and take that home to the extent that a pension had been given to the old person. That is quite a different situation, if the minister appreciates my point.

I would like to ask my
hon. friend a question. The purpose of the act is not to give anything to those who have some property now, but to give something to those who are almost destitute. If we have no pension plan such as this in operation, those relatives of the aged people will have to contribute, will they not? If that is so, and we relieve them of that burden, is it not fair that the pension authorities, or in other words the taxpayers of the country, should get back that money spent in relieving the relatives of their duty?

As the act is drafted it
covers a number of cases which would carry out the purpose of the government and be fair; but it also covers a number of cases which would foe very unfair. You would put a premium on extravagance; you would tell the old people of Canada that it is no use to save so long as this statute is in effect. They will get a. pension anyway, and they might as well spend their money on automobiles because after a while that money will be taken by the state. So I say the principle underlying that clause is fallacious and unsound, it does not encourage thrift; it is not to the advantage of the pensioner or the immediate relatives of the pensioner and is not of particular value to the state. I would suggest that an exemption similar to that in force in Australia be included, which would allow the old people to have property up to a certain amount. You can make provision that dependents having a natural duty or even a legal duty to provide for their parents and failing to do so could be deprived of sharing in the property.
There is another situation Which arises just at that point. Ontario and Quebec pay eighty per cent of the taxes of Canada. Supposing these two provinces do not accept this pension bill, while the western provinces and the more eastern provinces adopt it. Ontario and Quebec have homes for old people, as well as all kinds of charitable and benevolent institutions to relieve the needy. If this bill goes into effect and these two provinces refuse to accept it, they will then be in the position of paying eighty per cent of all the money contributed by the Dominion government to the other provinces, and in addition they will be paying for the maintenance of the old people of their own provinces. That is a fact which is very clear. What will be the consequence? When this legislation is presented to these provinces it is unlikely that they will accept it, and I do not see anything in this bill which makes provision enabling the province of Quebec, let us say, or the province of Ontario to take their share of this old age pension money and apply it to the institutions already in existence. They are now taking care of their aged in a scientific manner, and they may say they want to turn the money over to these institutions. Is there any provision by which such an arrangement might be made?

There is no such provision in this bill, which is identical with the bill we passed last session. I might also say that the government is trying to get the principle of old age pensions established and then they can see what amendments are necessary later on.

Why not find out now,
while we are preparing the legislation?
There are a lot of things we do not know yet.

When this bill went
through the House last year, in common with many others on this side of the House I advocated a federal measure. We do not need to rehearse our criticisms, but we said the bill was no good because it was unworkable, and so far I do not think we have changed our minds. But I have a suggestion which the minister might consider. My suggestion is that the federal government might bring in a succession duty tax which would probably make up the fifty per cent which the provinces should pay, and that would enable us to make it a strictly federal measure. I understand that we would be invading a provincial field1 of taxation there, but since we are assuming provincial burdens I think it would be fair and in addition to that this parliament would have absolute control over the pensions. I think that idea is workable, because the Dominion government could invade the provincial field of taxation in view of its assuming the fifty per cent obligation which the provinces would otherwise have to carry. If you adopt this suggestion you will make the proposed bill workable; I do not think it is workable as now contemplated.

What would be the effect of putting my hon. friend's suggestion into force, in view of the existing succession duties levied by the different provinces?
Old Age Pensions
Confiscation.
You could not put on an additional tax.
That would be in addition to the existing provincial tax.
Then in addition to the existing provincial succession duties, there would be a duty levied by the federal government under my hon. friend's proposition?

I do not want to get too far away from the main points I am endeavouring to present to the minister and which if not properly met will, I fear, be the undoing of this measure. In common with all other hon. members here I am desirous that an old age pension bill be passed. I wish not only that the bill should be passed but that it should become operative, and above all things that the people who are entitled to receive an old age pension should get their cheques. I made the prediction a year ago, and also two years ago, that under this measure the old folks of this country will not get their cheques. I repeat that prediction now. There are too many impracticable provisions in the proposed bill to permit of that being done. The outstanding one is the one I mentioned to the minister a moment ago.
Does my hon. friend refer to the provision transferring or taking the property of the aged pensioner?
That is one of them.

May I just call my hon. friend's attention, while he has his mind on that subject, to the fact that the provision in this bill is nearly identical with the provision which has prevailed for many years in Ontario with regard to indigents in houses of refuge? In that province if an indigent admitted to a house of refuge had any property, it was thought to be only fair such property should be available for the county houses of refuge. There was power vested in the county court judge, if the indigent ob-

jected to transferring the property, make the transfer to the county in trust for him, and if anything was left after meeting the cost of the indigent's maintenance in the institution the residue was to go to his estate. The county held that property in trust and the provision under which that procedure was adopted is, as nearly as possible the provision contained in the bill we propose to pass here. That is to say, if you are going to grant a pension to an aged person, his heirs, when they are making no provision for him, should not be permitted to receive the pensioner's property after his death.

The minister will note that in the case he has outlined the province provides the building in which the indigent person is housed, and everything else necessary for his care, but in the case of a pensioner under the scheme we are now considering there is nothing of that nature. A grant of money is supposed to be made to aged persons who use that money to maintain homes for themselves. The two sets of conditions are entirely different. In Australia they have adopted the principle of granting exemption to the pensioners. However, the point I have just been discussing is only one point. There are quite a number of points involved here. There is, for instance, the age provision, then there is the question of the transfer of a pensioner from one province to another. But above all there is this question and to this I should like to direct the attention of the minister:	How is he going to meet the
situation of these two great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which now pay eighty per cent of the taxation of this country and have institutions in which hundreds of thousands of dollars are invested for the maintenance and care of their old folks? What will happen to these institutions? In Quebec for example how are you going to distinguish * between aged persons in these institutions and other aged persons outside? Would it not be better if the federal and provincial authorities united in the common purpose of looking after old people, and utilized their joint forces towards that end? What will happen to the homes which are maintained by the provinces at the present time if they accept the old age pensions scheme? Would the minister entertain granting any concession by way of allowance to these governments to the extent of the responsibility involved by their maintaining indigent people in these homes?

We have bad a very interesting and instructive discussion on the resolution. Perhaps hon. gentlemen will permit us to make progress with it in order that the Min-
