ister of Labour will have an opportunity of introducing his bill. When the bill goes into committee it can be considered in detail.
No.

May I ask the minister a
question. I was not here when the resolution was discussed the other day and I should like to ask him-	*

Just a moment. If the
hon. gentleman will permit me I should like to reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). In the regulations pertaining to the bill it will be possible to provide for contributing towards the support of a person in a hospital or in a home.
Can you provide for making a contribution to the government which is paying for the maintenance of these persons?

The question of contributing towards the maintenance of a person in a home can be provided for by regulation after a conference with the particular province concerned as to how this should be done. I think hon. members might accede to the request of the Minister of Finance and pass the resolution in order that the bill might be introduced. There will be ample opportunity for discussion when the bill is in committee.

There are very few suggestions of the Minister of Finance I would not readily accept, especially in view of the budget he brought down yesterday, but before a bill is introduced the principles on which it is based must be considered. That is the time for making practical suggestions as to the proposed legislation in order that it may contain whatever ideas can be gathered from the collective wisdom of hon. members. That is why, in my judgment, discussion of the resolution is preferable. However, I have covered the points which I rose to make and may I say this in conclusion: The suggestions I have advanced are those about which very considerable discussion took place during the recent general election, and from the response of the audiences which I addressed it was clear to me that the average person throughout the country would like to see corrections made in the proposed pensions measure along the lines I have mentioned, especially with regard to the age at which persons should receive a pension, and in connection with this matter of old persons caTed for in homes. I ask the minister to give the most serious consideration to the suggestions and to embody some if not all of them in the bill whidh he proposes to introduce.

I am in favour of the principle of the proposed bill, but I rather concur in the remarks of my leader and of other hon. members on ithis side in favour of a federal scheme rather than the scheme outlined in the resolution. I do so because I see in this scheme delay and possible and very probable non-concurrence on the part of some of the provinces to the scheme, and in the future possible withdrawal of some of the provinces from the scheme, and consequent inequality and injustice, whereas I see in the federal scheme a scheme that will be administered by one body and that will therefore be much more simply and less expensively administered. I would put the age at sixty-five instead of seventy; I would raise the amount from $240 to $300, and I would make the maximum pension payable subject to reduction by the amount of the income of the pensioner in excess of $150 instead of $125 a year. I would also reduce the time limit in paragraph (d) to three years instead of five. I appreciate the fact that owing to the financial situation of the country that is a matter which can probably be dealt with much better in the future when our circumstances will permit, and that this is perhaps a good start. I therefore urge upon the government as strongly and emphatically as I possibly can in my humble capacity as a member, to change their minds, to drop the scheme as outlined in the resolution., and to bring in a bill providing for a federal scheme along the line that we on this side feel and so earnestly desire should be the measure put into effect.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. minister has told us that this is precisely the same bill as that brought down last session, and therefore the House and the country at large ought to be familiar with its provisions. Almost every hon. member who has spoken today has pointed out some objectionable feature in the bill, and it seems to me that if this measure is to be presented to the various provinces for acceptance, now is the time and this is the place to remedy these objections, instead of batting the question backwards and forwards between the provincial governments and Ottawa in an effort to arrive at a measure that will be acceptable to all.
I think that neither the customs scandal nor the tariff nor any ether issue in the last cam-
Old Age Pensions

paign received quite so much prominence as did this old age pension measure. It was a subject of discussion on practically every platform, and I expressed my strongest sympathy at that time, as I do now, with any measure for the relief of the aged. I do think, however, that there might be added to those who are to be benefited, the blind, and those who are crippled beyond the possibility of earning a livelihood. It seems to me that if there is one thing to commend this bill at all, it is merely that it paves the way to improved legislation. We might as well keep pace with the sister dominions in enacting an age limit of, say, 65 instead of 70, and most assuredly I think it would not be unreasonable for us to provide that ex-service men should come in at the age of 60. That has been a general request from the various local branches of the Canadian legion throughout Canada. I think that even the government will admit that this bill can be improved upon, and that now is the time and this is the place to do it, because if the provincial governments are to make amendments it will simply mean that the measure must come back to Ottawa, and its operation will be delayed for a full year.
I regret to say that in my district, as in other portions of British Columbia, practically every Liberal speaker took the opportunity to prejudice public opinion against Conservative candidates by the absolute assertion that the Conservative members at Ottawa had opposed this measure. In British Columbia the hon. Minister of Health in the federal cabinet was heralded as the father of the old age pensions bill. I presume, now that the Minister of Labour has the bill in hand, he will be acclaimed as its stepfather. However, neither of them can take very much pride in their offspring. The Minister of Health was in charge of the campaign in British Columbia, and I think that he too must answer for some rather gross misrepresentations concerning this measure, because I happen to have here a full page advertisement published by the hon. minister, or at least by his committee, in which his picture appears and in which he tells the people that "the old age pension bill provides $480 a year for the rest of their lives." That is what the Minister of Health, who I believe is also in charge of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, tells the people in this Cranbrook paper, his home paper-that the old age pension bill carries with it an annuity of $480.

So that there will be no misunderstanding, if my hon. friend will read the advertisement he will find that an

aged couple who had not means and were entitled to come under the act would receive under its provisions $480.
The advertisement says in plain English that the Liberal pension bill "provides $480 for the rest of their lives."
For an aged couple.

Into West Kootenay the
hon. minister brought from the city of Vancouver a breezy Liberal candidate by the name of Gale, who deliberately stated from the platform that his Conservative opponent voted against the old age pension bill. I do not charge that the hon. minister supplied this Liberal candidate with his ammunition,-I mean platform ammunition, of course, but the fact remains that he travelled with him, spoke from the same platform and assisted in his campaign, and never once did the hon, minister see fit to say that the statements made by his candidate were not correct. He was perfectly willing to let the public receive a wrong impression and allow his candidate to go to any extent in order to win that election. As I say, the minister was in charge of the campaign in British Columbia, and when the smoke of battle cleared away he was able to come back to his leader at Ottawa and say: "Behold, chief, I went into battle in British Columbia with ten Conservatives, and I have brought you back twelve. And I almost missed the train myself." ,So that when you consider the debilitated condition of the Liberal ranks in British Columbia it is not to be wondered that the Prime Minister saw fit to give to that province a Minister of Health. While we are at this stage it is rather peculiar to note the changed conditions, or the change of opinion, on the part of the government in connection with these ministers. I think it was last session that the Prime Minister made a statement, of course, from political expediency, that he was going to reduce the number of portfolios; and on page 1400 of Hansard he stated that the portfolios of soldiers' civil re-establishment and public health would be combined with some other department; in other words, that it was not of much importance and he would practically do away with it. Now the difficulty is that they cannot find enough portfolios to go round, and so they are creating still others.
All I have to say in connection with the old age pension bill, which was a matter of much discussion in West Kootenay district, is that if the ton of money spent by the fourteen Liberals in endeavouring to secure their own election had come out of their own pockets, they would have been so financially

Old Age Pensions
finished that they would! be the first fourteen applicants for the old age pension. If we are going to be in earnest in this thing, why not improve the measure now? What is the use of fooling the people any more? blame anybody for changing his mind from last year or two years ago, but I think if we looked around to find out how many members of this House have changed their minds on this question in the past two years, we should find that probably seventy-five per cent of them have. I regret it for more than one reason. But the chief reason why I regret it is that there may be provinces in the Dominion of Canada that will not accept the provisions as outlined in the bill of last year. It would be a cruel thing, Mr. Chairman, as I view it, if after what was said in the last election, after ail the promises that were held out by the Liberal party and by the Conservative party, there should be old people in some of the provinces who would not be in receipt of an old age pension. I do not think there could be anything more cruel than to give the old folks of this country, the aged and the needy, the idea that they were going to receive an old age pension, and then when the bill becomes law, so far as this parliament is concerned, there should still be thousands of people in some of the provinces who would not get an old age pension. I frankly admit that a bill which in its main provision provides for only a fifty per cent contribution by the federal exchequer is not going to meet with the approval of the provinces, and if I could urge anything upon the government it would be to increase that contribution from fifty to seventy-five per cent at least.

old age pensions. Nobody has outlined what is meant by a federal scheme. A federal scheme would involve federal administration, and personally I am in favour of provincial administration, because I believe that by provincial administration we are going to get more efficient administration. I believe that if my friends on the Liberal side of the House could express their feelings freely on this matter, we would have a good many hon. gentlemen sitting on the government side of the House who would be heartily in favour of a seventy-five per cent contribution from the federal exchequer to the scheme of old age pensions.

scheme that will give to the pioneers of confederation something that is worth while.

This House now accepts the principle of old age pensions, and not only has the principle been accepted by this House, but it has been accepted throughout the whole country. From one end of Canada to the other we find Liberals and Conservatives vieing with each other as to which can give to the old people of this country the better old age pension measure. There is one other question that I wish to touch upon before I sit down, and it appertains to the amount which an old man can earn outside of the amount which he receives as a pension. When we speak of a pension, I hope this matter is looked upon as a pension and not as a gratuity, as it is, I believe, considered by some hon. members. When men or women have reached the age of seventy years, having lived honourable lives and having given of their best to this Dominion, the least the state can do for them is to provide 
them with something to tide them over their difficulties in their old age, and that should not be looked upon as charity but as something the state owes them. An old lady hailing from Kingston came to see me in the city of Winnipeg where she was living on the gifts of her friends. She told me that her grandfather was one of the founders of the city of Kingston, and yet that old lady of about seventy-five years was compelled to go round and live on the charity of the people of the city of Winnipeg.
The bill as it came before us last year provided for a maximum earning, including the pension of $240 per annum, of $365 per annum. In other words, if a pensioner was earning more than $10.50 per month, he would have a reduction made from the amount of his pension. If he was earning $20 a month, his pension would be reduced by the amount which he earned over $125 a year. In other words, if he earned $240 per annum he would be entitled to a pension of only $125 per annum. That is one of the lowest amounts of any pension scheme that I know of in any part of the world. The limit has been practically wiped out of the old age pension legislation in Great Britain. The limit in Australia is considerably higher than that proposed in the bill which probably will come before us in the next few days. I hope the government will take into their serious consideration the question of increasing to $240 per annum the amount of earnings allowed in addition to the pension of $240.
I also hope they will take into consideration the question of increasing the grant from the federal treasury to the provincial treasury from fifty to seventy-five per cent. He suggested that the Minister of Labour should have discretionary powers to take in a man or a woman who was under the age of seventy, provided that he or she suffered from some physical disability. In other words, the Minister of Labour could, I suppose, by order in council or on his own initiative-I do not envy him his job-decide that someone was seventy when lie was only fifty-five. That is a most admirable position for someone around election time. I would point out that this measure is called an act respecting old age pensions. It is not an act respecting the blind which is a very worthy object and one that should be taken up some day, the sooner the better so far as I am concerned. It is not an act respecting cripples or those suffering from any other disability, nor even an act respecting soldiers. It is an act respecting destitute old people, and I think the act is big enough to be passed without our bringing in other aspects of disability with which it has nothing to do, but which tend to becloud the issue, increase enormously the expense and perhaps render the whole thing inoperative.
Another hon. member said that a pension of $20 per month was too little. I know it is; I agree with him that $20 a month is too little; but we must begin small and we know that it will never get less. One or two other hon. members said that the pension should be raised to at least $30 a month, nn increase of 50 per cent again. I will deal with those figures later on.
I think one hon. member from British Columbia stated that in our gaols we allowed a dollar a day for keeping each prisoner. Being more familiar perhaps with gaols than he is. I would point out that there is a reason for that. To begin with in gaols there is a certain amount of extra expense for fortifications, guards, bars and police that have to be provided. But there is another aspect of the matter and perhaps I am not giving away my province when I say this. There has been a movement there for some years past to induce the different municipalities who do their own policing, to turn over that obligation to the province, at a price, of course. The

Old Age Pensions
rAovement is gaining some headway and it is desirable from the point of view of the government that the3' get this all within their control. They think in that way they can control it better and do the work more cheaply than the municipalities. The price used to be only fifty cents a day and now they have raised it to a dollar. The reason is not because it costs a dollar now any more than it did before, but because it makes the municipalities more willing to turn over the responsibility to the province. That is the reason why they have jacked up the price of keeping a prisoner, which price of course has to be paid by the municipalities, to a dollar a day. It does not really cost as much as that to keep him.
An hon. member, from British Columbia again, trotted forward-no, he was ashamed to bring forward the argument he used in this connection on the platform, but he tried to cover it up in this way. He brought forward the question of a widow who was not a British subject before her marriage. On every platform in the campaign I was assailed by the idea that this legislation had deliberately and heartlessly legislated against the poor woman, say a Scandinavian who had come to this country and been a good, honest and faithful wife to a British subject for twenty years and who had raised a large family-the number varied from time to time-and then when her husband died no provision was made for her because she was an alien before her marriage. Some speakers were really ignorant, but hon. members knew that was a complete mis-statement of fact. None knew better that that was put in not to hurt any widows but to protect them. As I think someone explained this afternoon, it was put in to cover the case of a Canadian woman who married an American. As at least every lawyer knows she then takes the nationality of her husband, and therefore, when he dies, she still remains an American woman and ineligible for a pension. It was this case that the bill provided for. In that case she could in five years get back and renew her nationality with expense, worry and nothing to eat in the meantime. We provided that while she was technically an alien, an American, she was allowed to go back to her own British nationality. Therefore it was a very well thought out thing, but it was thrown against us that we were not taking care of the poor woman. In his desire this afternoon to confuse the issue, he said there might be a case, yes perhaps one in a thousand or five thousand- of a woman with a dual nationality where after the decease of her British husband she would still have
both a British and a Japanese or a German nationality. How many times would that occur in a thousand years? Any difficulty of course would be obviated by the fact that if she returned to Japan-and only in that way could she regain her Japanese nationality- she would cease to draw the pension.

My hon. friend seems reluctant to name members to whom he refers. I do not know why he lacks such courage. I ask him whether my statement of law with respect to the national status of dual citizenship is not correct, because he knows.

It is possibly correct that
a woman or man can have two nationalities, such as British and German. If they went back to Germany, they wmuld be Germans. The same might be true as regards Japan. It was the case until a year or two ago and probably it would be found that they could easily regain their Japanese nationality. But that could happen only if they left Canada, and if they leave Canada, this legislation says that they lose their pension anyhow. The chances of that happening would be one in a thousand. That was not the contention and well does the hon. gentleman know it. The contention made on the platform was that we were discriminating against a large number of decent people who had come into this country and married Canadians.

I wish to take exception,
on a question of privilege, to the remarks of the hon. member. That was the contention made and my hon. friend, whose casuistry and sophistry are so apparent on the platform, has sometimes to have these facts clearly stated. The contention which I made, and made in his constituency, was precisely the one I made in the House to-day, and none other.

I seem to have touched
somebody on the raw. Another criticism that was made on the platform was this. He said -I am reading from his own party paper:
The act they proposed said that pensions would be paid in accordance with regulations thereunder. The act was so involved in a technical way that nobody could get a pension under it.
In a technical way!
To obtain the pension a person had to confess to being 70 years of age.
Would not that be a terrible thing?
The women would not like that. They do not like to give their age.
Old Age Pensions

And so on, and so on. A moment later he [DOT] added:
The Senate did not kill the bill. All they did was to bury it. The Liberals' old age pension bill was a sham and was designed solely as a vote catcher.
That is the bill which he now says he is heartily supporting!
There is one other clause with which I would like to deal. I think this was the section which he referred to as the most damning in the whole act, and that is section 9. That is the one which empowers the board to claim the estate of a deceased pensioner under certain conditions. I think he used the language-I took it down at the time-that this meant confiscation under all circumstances. That will show in Hansard tomorrow if it is put down as I heard it. I think the hon. minister questioned the accuracy of his statement, and I think he then modified it, but that was his original statement which would have gone out to the country without contradiction if the minister had not risen-that this section meant confiscation under all circumstances.

The hon. gentleman is as incapable of clearly stating the facts here as he was on the hustings in his own constituency. I did not say that. The section is quite clear as to what is meant. I explained very clearly the nature of the effect of the section which I described as being a confiscatory section, calculated to confiscate the home, which it does, but not confiscation under all circumstances. Such a contention is clearly ridiculous.

Hansard, if it has not been
tampered with, will reveal the truth tomorrow.

Mr. Chairman, I ask the
hon. gentleman to withdraw that.
Hansard is not tampered with. The idea of any man suggesting that!

The hon. gentleman from
Comox-Alberni may indulge in that practice, but I do not. I ask that the hon. gentleman withdraw that statement, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I personally did not
hear the hon. gentleman make that statement. If he did make the statement which he will know himself, I think in fairness to the reportorial staff he should withdraw it.
What I meant was this, Mr. Chairman. It is a well known custom that we are allowed to revise our speeches to make them read a little better, by putting in a word here or extracting a word there.
That is not tampering.

What I meant was that if
the statement has not been corrected, Hansard will show that it was as I have stated. I had no intention whatever-I cannot emphasize this -too strongly-of making any reflection on the reportorial staff.

Would it not be wise, Mr. Chairman, to ask the hon. gentleman to express his views on old age pensions without doing so mudh quibbling about what certain hon. members said on the hustings in the province of British Columbia? I am sick of listening to this sort of thing all day. It is a shame to be wasting the time of the House listening to such bunk, and it is pure bunk. The hon. member should not be listened to at all. He is quite capable of expressing himself on the subject of old age pensions. He did it in the committee, and he should keep to the subject before the Chair. We should not have to listen to this.
It was not the hon. gentleman who has just sat down who had to suffer from these unfair allegations in the campaign.

It is taking the
time of the House that should not be taken.

I was going on to explain
about this case of a deceased pensioner. I really think it is deserving of being explained in the fullest way. It has been alleged that after the man dies, the government steps in and takes his property. What are the facts? He can leave it to any other pensioner he likes. He does not need to be a blood relation or anything of that kind. If he has a little property he can leave it to an old friend or chum as long as it goes to help the scheme, which in turn will be able to pay bigger pension later on. That is all right. Then they are allowed to leave it to any one who has helped them in their old age by ever so little. It does not even need to be in cash. It says in cash or otherwise, I think. Supposing a man says: "Well, there is an old couple, and their pension is not very big. I have a cottage that I do not need very much, and I will let them have it rent free." It would apply to that. Or a son might not be able to give a cash contribution, but he might be able to give house-room to his father or mother or his mother-in-law. In a case like that, however little the contribution was, if it was at all a genuine attempt to carry out his filial obligations, he would be allowed to get the full amount of what the deceased pensioner left.

Old Age Pensions
One hon. gentleman opposite-I will not put it nearer than that, to save interruptions- asked, what about the grandchild? The hon. member suddenly produced a grandchild of the pensioner, who is in a state of destitution also, and when the old man died, who was to keep the grandchild? 1 recall in one of Mrs. Nellie McClung's books a lady speaking on the platform on behalf of the franchise for women, and some man said, "It would never do. Who would mind the baby while the woman wen; out to vote?" And the lady replied with a good deal of aptness, "Why, I think I could get the same person to mind the baby that minds it when I go out to pay my taxes." I think the same thing is true here. I think the same people who were keeping this grandchild before the old man died would continue to keep it after his death. They could not have been living on the old man. If they were totally destitute, they would have been looked after in the home, or taken care of in some private family.
We have a branch of the federal government which is devoted wholly to endeavouring to get people in this Canada of ours to buy annuities. Why should we do that? It is a case of a man taking all his money and handing it over to the government and getting a certain annuity for life.
No. He pays weekly or monthly contributions as the case may be.
He can pay it in a lump sum if he likes.
Yes, if he has the money.

Should we discourage that because when he dies his grandchild will have nothing to get at all? Why not oppose that too? Let me give you an instance that comes home to both of us, and this is in British Columbia, with w'hich we are more familiar. When the hon. gentleman talks about this iniquitous clause that is going to damn this bill, does he know or does he not know, or will he not tell, that in British Columbia we have what is called an Old Men's Home, and you get admission to it by somebody-usually the municipalities-undertaking to pay so much. Sometimes if the people are without the scope of a municipality the government takes them in free. But before that poor old man goes to that home he has to sign over to the government not only all the property he possesses, such as his land or something of that kind, but all the property he may ever become possessed of. He may come into a fortune while in the Old Men's Home, but it is all assigned and turned over to the government when he dies. I am not saying that that is a good scheme
but I am saying that the scheme in the bill was a good deal better than that because we did allow the man's property to go to his friends, relations and so on.
Does my hon. friend know of a similar clause in the legislation of Great Britain?
As to the government receiving deceased pensioners' estates?
Yes.

I do not know. I want to sum up from the point of view of making it a federal scheme. As we know, the difficulty is the high cost. Now, let us lump the whole criticism together and see where we stand. As we know, it was partly the high cost that made its passage doubtful in the other House last year. Now it is proposed to make the scheme purely a federal one. It was estimated last year that it would cost $11,500,000 a year. Making it a purely federal scheme would bring the cost to $23,000,000. Let us accept that. Let us also accept the suggestion that we should give this relief to people sixty years of age. That would increase it ninety per cent and bring the cost up to $43,700,000. Then we come to the hon. member who says that we should raise it from $20 to $30 a month. That would bring the cost up to $66,500,000. Then there is the whole of the administration cost. Of course if we take it over as a federal scheme we will have to run it ourselves. Then there were one or two other minor suggestions which, if adopted, would bring the cost up to $70,000,000; that is, if we accept the various suggestions which have been made, and the government has been urged to accept them in a fair spirit of criticism, that would mean (hat the cost would be nearly $70,000,000. What does that mean? It means that the bill would never pass this House, would never pass the Senate and would never pass the country. The result would be that the very object of the bill to give relief to the old people would be nullified entirely, because we would never get anywhere with a proposal to expend $70,000,000 annually on the scheme.

Being a new member of the House, Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to discuss in any way the old age pension scheme, as I am not familiar with the clauses of the bill. I have listened to the discussion with the greatest care, hoping to gain from it an elucidation of the clauses of the resolution that has been introduced. The mass of
Old Age Pensions

material presented to ns to-night has reminded me of a well-known fable. A deer, having been wounded in the forest, retired to a comfortable shady place where there were enough luscious grass and tender leaves to keep him from hunger and starvation until his wounds were healed. But a great number of his friends came from the surrounding forest to sympathize with him, and one suggested one thing and one another in order to give him relief. They consoled and sympathized with him in his sickness, but it was not long until that deer died-not from his wounds but from starvation. And so it seems with the old age pension scheme.
I would not have risen to-night had I not heard one thing in particular that the Minister of Railways said. After this discussion we are convinced that the position of the Conservative party has been emphatically and clearly enunciated-that they are behind this scheme for old age pensions, whether it be under federal control or in conjunction with the provinces. I wish the minister were here to correct me if I am wrong, because I wrote down the words he uttered. In referring to this matter he said that they, the opposition, were not in favour of the old age pension scheme unless after consultation with the various provincial legislatures. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that words bearing that meaning were uttered in this House by hon. members on this side. If they were, Mr. Chairman, I would oppose the proposition, because personally I feel that we are wasting precious time on a matter in respect to which there is absolute unanimity, and such unanimity has been expressed in this House tonight.
I was impressed by the words of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I felt that he expressed what must have taken place in this House last year when he said there was a great difference of opinion in regard to different clauses of the bill. However, I think we have reached the stage now that it is not a question of the clauses of the bill, because these can be discussed when the bill comes before us. It is not a question of what took place on the hustings last year nor a question of reading reports from lastt year's speeches which have no relation to the question now before the House. The question is, are we decided, are we unanimous that this old age pension scheme should be put into force and that even if not perfect, it will be given a chance. That is the question, Mr. Chairman, and I have heard the leader of the opposition emphatically say that we were behind it if it were decided that the provincial
[Mr. Brad v. I
legislatures should participate in the scheme with the federal government. I regret that we have had so much sophistry and so much discussion; it makes it look to me as if we are not sincere. What does it matter who is to have the honour of passing the old age pension scheme? The point is that throughout the length and breadth of Canada there are people waiting for the verdict of this House. Them we must consider, not whether it shall be a bill of ten clauses or a bill of twenty clauses, but a bill pledged to these people, an old age pension scheme.

I would not rise to address the committee at this late hour were it not -that in the recent election there was so much misrepresentation of the Conservative party and of certain members thereof in this House during the last session on the subject now under consideration. So great was that misrepresentation that it is absolutely essential that in self defence at least one should offer some observations in respect of the matter.
It is for instance very much to be regretted that an hon. gentleman in one of the Ontario constituencies charged that I opposed the old age pensions bill. Nothing is more certain than this, that if under our democratic institutions it is impossible to discuss in parliament a measure of this kind without liability to a charge of opposition to the measure itself, then indeed the value of those institutions, the value of parliament will have passed, and we shall have become mere rubber stamps, registering the will of governments. It is of the utmost importance that every phase of a question of this character should be thoroughly discussed. I find on consulting Hansard of last year, at page 1975, that I spoke as follows:
I apologize for trespassing again to-night upon the time of the House, but I feel very strongly on this subject. I am deeply interested in it; I desire to see it succeeed. I am convinced that it cannot succeed without the co-operation of all the provinces, unless the Dominion, in defiance of our constitutional jurisdiction as voiced by the Deputy Minister of Justice, sees fit to undertake the whole responsibility, which would involve us in an expenditure of $23,000,000 per annum.
I said that because I had previously read the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice -with which, of course, I did not necessarily agree-that there was some question as to our constitutional power in the premises. But I pointed out that if the bill as then introduced by the Minister of Public Works of the day, acting as Minister of Labour, had passed into law, no single individual in Can-

Old Age Pensions
ada could have benefited by the legislation. And on the hustings the Conservative party repeated that statement. For it is a fact that cannot be denied that had that measure been passed by the Senate and given the royal assent, becoming a statute, there was not a single individual in Canada who would have received one cent under it. And why? Because not a single province had enacted old age pensions legislation.
Now there is this to be said, and every hon. member will, I am sure, seriously consider it. To what extent should the parliament of Canada by legislation enforce its will upon provincial legislatures? That is a question that affects the whole structure of our constitutional system, and if we enact statutes whereby we declare that a certain class of people within the province may receive the benefits of federal legislation only on condition that the province shall refrain from crossing a single "t" or dotting an "i,'? merely doing what we tell them to do, then the provincial legislatures are deprived of the very power which, under our constitution, they should possess. And this statute proposes to make those provincial legislatures, who desire to avail themselves of the advantages of this law, nothing more nor less than registering automatic machines to carry out the will of this parliament. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. We are imposing our will upon the provincial legislatures.
What does the hon. member mean by imposing our will upon them? There is no provincial legislature which is bound to accept this proposal.

Surely my hon. friend
with his astuteness sees that that is the very point I am making. No legislature is bound to accept the proposal, but if it does it must accept it in its entirety without crossing a "t" or dotting an "i". It must take the measure as it is presented by this parliament. In other words, as I say, this parliament imposes its will on the legislature of any province that accepts the measure.
Would the will of parliament not be more wholly enforced upon the province if the scheme were a purely federal one?

Yes, because every federal statute is of dominion wide application; in its operations it extends to every part of the country. But that is the important difference; for a federal statute does not leave its application to the will of any provincial legislature, either t.o accept or to reject its terms. I was happy the other evening to hear the observations of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), who was in the House when the committee reported on this subject originally a couple of years ago. That report, following on the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, was predicated upon the idea that a provincial conference would be held so that we might arrive at some definite conclusion whereby we could prepare a satisfactory measure to place upon the statute books, a measure that would have federal application. The difference between a federal and a provincial statute i* this:	one is operative solely within tne
boundaries of the province, while the federal statute applies to the Dominion at large. If therefore the province is compelled to accept a measure passed by this parliament, or, on the other hand, to decline it in toto, then the legislative power of that province is curtailed and restricted to that extent, and its legislators no longer exercise their jurisdiction but are subject to the will of this body. My hon. friend (Mr. Heaps) will clearly see that. That 'being so we did point out last year that under the circumstances it was desirable that a conference should be held. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) the other evening read into Hansard an observation of mine, dissociated from its text, in which I asked the Prime Minister not to force the measure last year. I implored him to take steps to see that the report of the committee should be carried out and a conference of representatives of the provinces held, so that some measure of uniform application might be drawn up. But it was charged throughout the country from one end to the other, and in some of the Ontario constituencies particularly, that the Minister of Finance was opposed to old age pensions. I can only repeat what I have just now read. If anyone will take the trouble to refer to Hansard and to read in its entirety the observations I made in this regard-I hope no one will do anything of the sort-he will find that I gave a considerable amount of attention to the matter. I had had an opportunity of studying the subject at first-hand in England, and after many inquiries I had obtained a good deal of information. There were two classes of cases to be dealt with: one, the case of those over seventy years of age who would get the benefit of the legislation if the provinces passed an old age .pensions measure. I urged a contributory system and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was good enough to felicitate me on what he graciously described, as my helpful observations. The matter was not of a controversial nature. But I realized that under any contributory system
Old Age Pensions

there are in every country numbers of men and women between the ages of sixty-five and seventy who would find it impossible to make any contributions, not having the financial ability to do so. And in the very closing words of my remarks, which I made to the House on that occasion, I used the following language which I now desire to repeat:
T think the government, therefore, will be well advised perhaps to release the whip on its own members and let the opinion of the House as a whole determine whether or not it is desirable at this session to push into this matter or, in the light of a subsequent conference between the provincial and Dominion authorities, arrive at a conclusion which will enable us to place on our statute books legislation of a character that will redound to the credit of this country and that will maintain the confidence and self-respect of the future citizens of this Dominion by encouraging the practice of economy and thrift, while providing for the aged of to-day by suitable contributions to provincial schemes.
That is to say, in order to meet the case of those who could not immediately make contributions because of financial inability, we should ourselves make the necessary grant of money under the circumstances. I referred at that time to a speech of the Hon. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, to show that miHions of pounds were involved in the scheme in operation in England, and at the same time I mentioned- the observations of Neville Chamberlain u-pon the same matter.
Now, let us for a moment forget all about the past. It is not a matter of great importance to me that I was misrepresented. I do not care except for the fact that I owe a duty to friends of mine to correct wrong impressions of this character. I am quite content that the record should speak for itself and I am not concerned about what was said in the late elections. I am however concerned that we should have a clear appreciation and a full understanding of just what we are doing in this legislation. We are not granting old age pensions. That is number one. That, we have said in this resolution, is to be done by the provinces. All we are doing is to place upon the statutes books a provision whereby a sum of money will be granted to any province that sees fit to pass legislation in terms set forth by us. That, to all intents and purposes, is a federal scheme, without having the advantages and benefits of a federal scheme. In the province of Alberta it was a Labour member of the legislature who moved its rejection although at present, the Alberta legislature is giving the matter further consideration.	It was
Mr. White, Labour member from the city

of Calgary, who moved the resolution in the legislature condemning this provincial legislation, and I have found out since why that was done. It was done because they said, "This is a very simple matter; you are endeavouring to pass this on to the municipalities, and that is just what the municipalities do not want you to do." They say that "If this is to be a scheme let it be a federal scheme; if there is to be such a scheme let the Dominion take the responsibility for it, and do not endeavour to place the responsibility on the provinces and deny them the right to formulate their own scheme. Do not give them a grant of money without permitting them to have something to say in the matter." That is the situation, and there can be no doubt about it; anyone who reads the bill or the resolution will find that that is so.
I regret to say further that during the last election one of the successful candidates, now sitting in this House, published an advertisement in which he pointed out that it was a " board of strategy " which induced gentlemen in another chamber to destroy the bill. Misrepresentations of that character are not calculated to enhance the value of our institutions. Mr. Meighen has said publicly on many occasions, and he is not now here to repeat it, that he had no part in what happened, nor wias he advised of it. He has further said that it was against his protests, when he did hear of it, that the action took place in another chamber which resulted in disaster to that measure. This side of the House gave its support to that measure after pointing out its weaknesses; we did not ask for a division, and for myself I then stated, as I now state, that I believe in an old age pension scheme. But I do not believe in an old age pension scheme based upon a mere granting of money to a provincial authority, thus imposing our views upon them willy nilly. There must be an exercise of some legislative discretion by these legislatures if they desire to pass a measure of this kind, but that is denied them; they must either accept or reject. They must take it as it is or drop it; they cannot get a sou unless they take it as we give it to them, and if they take it in that way they may get some money. That is the position, and that is what the leader of this party pointed out the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I ask a question? In
what respect does this measure differ from the act giving aid to agriculture and the good roads assistance, which were supported by my hon. friend in 1913 and 1914?

Old Age Pensions

I was going to begin my answer by calling my hon. friend my dear friend; I feel almost affection for him, because I have known him so long, and he is always kindly and courteous. The fact that someone passed legislation with respect to agriculture and highways does not in any sense make this legislation good;, because there was a conference with respect to those measures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no conference.

Pardon me, but I happened to be present, in a very unofficial way, at one of those conferences. I do not know whether or not all of the provinces were represented, but I do know that many of them were.
Surely, my hoD. friend will not say that the provinces agreed to the terms of that federal legislation?

I am coming to that. The provinces were granted aid for highways and agriculture because the highways were of an interprovincial character, and were so intended to be. My friends will recall the circumstances; 'it was felt that great trunk highways of an interprovincial character, which really had a federal aspect, should be assisted out of the federal treasury, and the conditions under which assistance should be given were laid down by regulation and agreement. With respect to agriculture the position is that under the British North America Act jurisdiction is given both the province and the Dominion, and the Dominion has been steadily granting aid to agriculture. But there came a time when some of the provinces urged that the obligations of a local character were so vast that they desired aid from the federal treasury, and this aid was granted under conditions which were agreed to by the representatives of the federal and provincial authorities. But that is a very different situation from that which now confronts us. Here all we are doing is placing on the statute books a provision by which a grant is to be made, covering half the money paid for old age pensions, but the terms and conditions under which the provinces will have to carry on their scheme are fixed by us.
As in the other cases.

In those cases the terms were fixed by regulation and agreement, but this is a measure which says willy nilly, "Accept or reject." If they Teject, what happens? The difficulty is that they still pay.
Mr. KING (Kootenay). The conditions are the same as in those other cases.

But in the other cases
all the provinces availed themselves of the benefits of the legislation.
They will do the same in this case.

But the point I desire to make is that which was pointed out by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) last year. First of all you should not have this parliament thus imposing its will on the provinces, and giving them no discretion at all; then, if we are going to make a grant of money and impose the terms under which it may be used, let us have our own scheme and not a hybrid plan, partly provincial and partly federal. That is the position, and that is the reason my leader made his observations the other evening with regard to this matter, with which I wholly agree. I say to this House that there is no chance of a proper scheme with respect to old age pensions being made successful by the provinces without making further demands upon the federal treasury. In that regard I have had the advice of men who do not live in this country at all; they have studied the question from every aspect and tell me that if we desire to make the scheme a success, it cannot possibly be done by the provinces alone. As was pointed out in the Alberta legislature, the burden would be passed on to the municipalities and added to the tax bills, so it must in the long run be borne by further applications made to the federal authorities. That is the position* as I see it with respect to this matter.
So far as I am concerned, notwithstanding the evident and manifest difficulties in the way, having pointed out this situation I propose to support this measure, but I do so only after bringing to the attention of the House the inevitable consequences. It was a great English statesman who said that under our modern democracy if one was right be could never afford to say so, because that invited a certain situation which brought about a great many difficulties. I will not elaborate the statement, but some day I will read the exact words to the House, because I think they will be of interest.

It reminds one of the advertisements sometimes seen in newspapers, wherein someone says that someone else has said very offensive things which are not true. May I ask the hon. member a question? I would say that at the moment we have placed our views as to this legislation before this parliament and the Canadian people. Until every legislature in Canada acts each province will or will not have an old age pension depending upon the action of that legislature, and there may be one province that has and another province that has not. That is the reason the suggestion was made by the leader of the opposition the other evening. I am most desirous there should be placed upon the statute books of this country a measure that is workable and useful. There are two considerations to be borne in mind. First of all we must consider those who are coming up to manhood and growing older, and secondly the class that can no longer contribute. I believe in a contributory system-I have never hesitated to say that I believe in it. The father of the old age pensions scheme of England said that without it you are doing a great injury to the very people whom you would benefit. I believe that; my reading induces me more and more to believe it is right. When the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) speaks of annuities I venture again to point out what I referred to last year and it is (this-that a small contribution made by men from month to month and week to week that will ensure them an annuity at sixty-five or seventy years of age is one of the most desirable things that you can have in any country. It is true (hat the Australian system has been changed, and they have now gone on a contributory basis. That is what happened in Australia where a non-contributory system was abandoned and the contributory system insisted upon. Because where you have each individual making some contribution he begins to realize what I endeavoured to say yesterday, that all contributions by the state mean taxation, and an expenditure of the money of the people, great or small, poor or rich. That is what I desire to make clear to this House. What I rose to say was I think it is highly desirable that we should have at least not to assert that men in this House oppose measures which they supported merely for the sake of getting a little support from those who are vitally affected. I suffered from it; other hon. members suffered from it. Old Age Pensions
It has been stated here time and time again, last year and this year, that we were wholly in favour of a workable scheme of old age pensions, but surely this parliament has not come to the pass where, to use the minister's own words-which I wrote down, we are "either for or against this bill"-we must either take a particular legislative proposal or leave it. Is this parliament reduced to the position that any minister of the crown can walk in here with a measure, lay it on the table, and then say to this honourable House-take it or leave it? Are we to be muzzled? Are we not to be permitted at least to scrutinize the language of the measure?
I have under my hand the full record of this House upon this question of old age pensions. I have here all the dates for the last fifteen years when this measure has been brought up, and in every instance it was brought up by a Conservative, until recent years, when the Labour party was represented in the House and it was brought up by them. In season and out of season for seventeen years I have supported in this House an old age pension bill. Long before my hon. friend ever entered the House, long before other hon. gentlemen over there entered who have been indulging in some rather extravagant language during this evening's session in attempting to castigate this party I supported and urged for an old age pension scheme. I have quotations here from Hansard where I questioned and urged and pleaded with the Hon. Mr. Murdock, a former Minister of Labour, to bring in an old age pension scheme. A committee was appointed, and my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin, formerly from East Calgary, took a very important part in its deliberations. We have in season and out of season-not the whole party, not every member, but a sufficiently large percentage of the party, speaking with some responsibility-urged for an old age pension scheme.
What we said to the government last year and what we say again this year is that in our opinion this proposal will not work satisfactorily, and because we are convinced of that we urged last year, and we have suggested again this year, that an effort should be made to have a measure that will be assured of success. The day I left Vancouver, Mr. Chairman, two elderly ladies-I should say they were seventy years of age-came to my office, and pleaded with me to do what I could for old age pensions. They did not know much about parliamentary practice. They had the idea that a member of parliament had some mysterious power that he could exercise to secure this measure. All
I could say to them, and all that hon. members of this House have been able to say is: We will do our best to get a measure through. We are anxious to get that measure. We are told to-night by the Minister of Health-he is not in his seat at the moment-that this measure will be supported by all the provinces. Now I am going to quote the Minister of Agriculture. There has been a lot of quoting done here to-night, and this is what he said, as reported in the Vancouver Daily Star, a strong and respectable and reliable Liberal paper, in its issue of August 25th:
Dealing with old age pensions Mr. Motherwell said the measure had met a sad fate at the hands of the Senate. He was sorry to say the Conservatives had obstructed the bill at all times.
Hear, hear. What are you doing now?

There has been, I have
noticed, during this sitting a good deal of hilarity and laughing over this matter, but I do not think it is a laughing matter at all, Mr. Chairman. It is a very, very serious matter. He went on to say:
If the people have to wait until the provinces are united to co-operate with the Dominion in the operation of an old age pension, then we will not get any pensions during the present generation.
Well?

I believe the minister is
right, if we have to wait until the provinces co-operate with the Dominion under the terms of this bill, we will not have old age pensions for a generation. That is my opinion and I expressed it last year. It is the opinion, Mr. Chairman, that we have been trying to impress upon the minds of the ministry. We-stated through my leader at the opening of' this session that if we had an old age pension bill that was under the jurisdiction of the; Dominion we might be certain it would be successfully applied, but if as the Minister of Public Works now says, we have either to take this bill or leave it-in other words if we are to be branded as opposed to the whole scheme of old age pensions if we criticise this bill-then we are prepared to accept it, but to do so after pointing out to the minister that in our opinion it will not achieve what it is pretended to the people it will achieve, namely, pensions for the aged. We are telling the minister that, and I hope that as the years go by and as hundreds, yes, thousands of people in this country are disappointed at not being able to receive a pension under this bill, it will be remembered, just as keenly remembered as some other statements of ours that we have made in this

parliament, that we warned parliament it would not work successfully as a measure.
Now there are clauses in the bill I would like to discuss. There are ellauses which obviously are not fair. There is one Clause in particular that has been cited here to-night, and I think if the people of Canada fully realized it they would not for one moment support the bill. I refer to the clause providing that the maximum pension shall be $240, and if any person applying for a pension is in receipt of an income in excess of $125, the increase, whatever it is, shall be deducted from that pension. Let me put it in plain, simple language; as one of the ministers said a minute ago, it means that if any applicant for a pension of $240 happens to have a meagre annual income of $200, he will not receive $240, but will receive $240 less $75, namely, $165. In other words it means that any person who, with the pension, can gather together $365, that is all he will get, including the pension. The thing is preposterous on the very face of it. There are other features of the bill that might very properly be criticised, but if we criticise it the minister says we are against the bill.
Not at all.

If we offer suggestions we are against the bill and we must be branded through the country as against the principle. We are either for it or against it. I am wholly in favour of the bill in so far as it deals with the principle of old age pensions, but I say again that the measure as now presented and presented in the House last year will not achieve the result which the minister said it would achieve.

speechtext:
Since the opening of the session the House has made very fair progress and the government appreciate the co-operation of hon. members opposite. The question now before the House involves the principle of an old age pension. I gather from the debate to-day that the House is practically unanimous on this measure. We have reached the time in Canada when we might have an old age pension. This measure involves the principle of an old age pension. After the resolution has been passed we will introduce the bill, and we can debate details later. I am told that this is the third time this resolution has been 'before parliament this session. We have debated this question all afternoon. It is now fifteen minutes after eleven when I think we should all be getting home and going to bed on a Friday night. If hon. members are prepared 
to allow the resolution to go through so that the bill may be introduced and we will learn what the measure is I think it would be wise. If further debate is desired then I shall ask my colleague to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I think the minister
will agree with me that the time which has been occupied in the discussion of this measure has not been lost, as it will shorten the time which we usually take in the discussion of a bill when in committee after the second reading. It matters very little, I think, so far as the consumption of time is concerned whether the discussion takes place now or on the second reading of the bill. It is not likely to take place again. I think the discussion has been very useful, notwithstanding the rather provocative speeches by the three ministers of the crown who have spoken at great length to-night on the measure. The discussion on this side of the House has been entirely sympathetic.
Not at all provocative.

Not at all provocative,
and I think we made it as clear as it could be made that that is the position we occupy. We are prepared to accept and pass this measure, not as a perfect measure at all, but, as I said a day or two ago, it is apparently the only thing the government is willing to give, and it is on that condition we are willing to pass it. I have no objection to the committee rising and reporting this resolution, but I cannot agree that there will not be further discussion when the bill is in committee of the whole.
